channel.title: Reviews Feed
channel.description: Aggregated reviews from Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology, Nature Reviews Genetics, Trends in Genetics, and Trends in Cell Biology.

item.title: Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology: The nucleocytoplasmic actin circuit in genome maintenance
item.description: The authors propose that nuclear actin levels are maintained through a regulatory circuit involving the DNA damage response, condensates, and transcriptional replenishment.

item.title: Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology: The integration of protein and organelle degradation systems and its pathophysiological functions
item.description: Removal of defective or excessive proteins and organelles is controlled by the ubiquitin–proteasome system and by autophagy pathways. This Review discusses the interplay between these degradation processes in response to physiological demands and cellular stresses and their pathological relevance.

item.title: Trends in Cell Biology: The Five Phases of cancer cells
item.description: Beyond identifying individual malignant hallmarks, the central challenge in cancer biology is to uncover the fundamental organizing principles that underlie the interactive nature of cancer cell behavior. Here, we transform the ancient Wuxing theory into a mechanistically grounded, hypothesis-generating biological framework that conceptualizes cancer cell biology around five mutually interacting processes: Pliability, Hybridity, Aggressivity, Sociability, and Evolutivity (PHASE). By engaging in the circuit of mutual promotion and restriction, these phases form an integrated regulatory system that provides a rationale for organizing diverse malignant properties. Within this framework, cancer traits emerge as context-dependent manifestations of the proposed core interactions. Collectively, PHASE offers a complementary perspective for understanding disease progression that could advance interaction-guided therapeutic strategies to target human cancers.

item.title: Trends in Genetics: The trans-acting potential of expanded repeat RNA
item.description: In a subset of repeat expansion disorders, nuclear dysfunction extends beyond the originating locus through poorly understood mechanisms. Studies from the C9orf72 gene indicate that repeat RNAs interact with the genome in trans, suggesting that disease-specific repeat RNA sequences and structures may similarly contribute to pathogenic mechanisms in some of these disorders.

item.title: Trends in Cell Biology: A tug-of-war in the niche: balancing forces to preserve stemness
item.description: Stem cell niches are mechanically self-regulating systems. Segú Cristina and colleagues show that reciprocal adhesion between glial niche cells and neural stem cells buffers tensile forces, preserving nuclear and mitotic integrity and sustaining stem cell proliferation. They identify immunoglobulin complexes as critical mechanoregulators, linking adhesion, tissue mechanics, and stemness.

item.title: Trends in Cell Biology: Decoding the functional specificity of E2F3 isoforms
item.description: E2F3 is a central regulator of cell cycle progression, development, differentiation, and oncogenesis. Alternative promoter usage generates two major homologous isoforms, E2F3A and E2F3B, differing only at their N-termini. Although E2F3A is traditionally considered an activator and E2F3B a repressor of transcription, studies suggest that both isoforms have overlapping and isoform-specific functions, shaped by differences in temporal expression, protein stability, and target gene specificity. In this review, we examine how E2F3A and E2F3B contribute to proliferation, differentiation, and cancer. We also discuss contradictions and limitations in experimental approaches that have complicated the interpretation of these functions. Finally, we explore how clarifying these roles could help resolve long-standing questions in cell cycle regulation, differentiation, and cancer, where E2F3 plays a major role.

item.title: Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology: Phosphatidylinositol 3,4-bisphosphate is a novel lipid helper for mitochondrial fusion
item.description: Golgi-derived vesicles that contain phosphatidylinositol 3,4-bisphosphate facilitate mitochondrial fusion at sites marked with mitofusins and endoplasmic reticulum.

item.title: Nature Reviews Genetics: Genomics for chronic overlapping pain conditions
item.description: Genomic studies are revealing shared genetic susceptibility across chronic pain conditions traditionally viewed as distinct disorders. In this Comment, Wainberg et al. argue that these findings support the concept of nociplastic pain and have important implications for disease classification, clinical trials and therapeutic development.

item.title: Nature Reviews Genetics: Sequencing and analysis of the human adaptive immune receptor repertoire
item.description: This Review examines how T cell and B cell receptor repertoires are generated and shaped by genetic variation, surveys experimental and computational approaches for their analysis and highlights emerging applications, recent advances and key challenges in adaptive immune receptor repertoire research.

item.title: Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology: Mechanisms and regulation of proteolytic DNA–protein crosslink repair
item.description: DNA–protein crosslinks (DPCs) obstruct essential chromatin processes, and their removal is crucial for genome stability. This Review discusses the origin and properties of DPCs, mechanisms of proteolytic DPC repair, and how defective DPC proteolysis contributes to genome instability, premature ageing and disease.

item.title: Trends in Genetics: Advancing microbial pangenomics through human pangenomics
item.description: Although the term pangenome originated in the study of microbial species, recent advances in eukaryotic pangenomics have been driven largely by the need to manage the substantial computational challenges posed by population-scale eukaryotic datasets. This review evaluates the extent to which existing eukaryotic pangenome tools and methods can be extended to microbial species. We first survey current eukaryotic and microbial pangenomic approaches and then examine opportunities and challenges in adapting eukaryotic methods to microbial genomes, with particular emphasis on scalability, data quality, evolutionary complexity, and benchmarking. Finally, we highlight areas where existing approaches generalize well and where substantive redesign and redevelopment are needed.

item.title: Trends in Cell Biology: Ultrastructure of multiciliated cell basal bodies revealed by expansion microscopy
item.description: van Grinsven et al. combine tenfold expansion microscopy with a volumetric fluorescence averaging tool to map the human airway basal body at nanoscale resolution. They resolve the 3D organization of more than 20 proteins and assess the function of a subset of proteins in the organization of the apical microtubule network.

item.title: Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology: Similar small RNAs, different biological outcomes
item.description: Similar small RNAs in Caenorhabditis elegans pair with different Argonaute proteins, resulting in differential targeting of nucleic acids and biological outcomes.

item.title: Nature Reviews Genetics: Tracing cell fate in space and time with SPACE-seq
item.description: In this Tools of the Trade article, Yuemeng Jia describes SPACE-seq. By combining lineage tracing with spatial transcriptomics, SPACE-seq connects lineage history to molecular state and tissue context, enabling insight into how tissue niches shape cell fate and clonal behaviour.

item.title: Trends in Cell Biology: Emerging roles of microtubules in directional cardiomyocyte remodeling
item.description: Past research has long hinted at a connection between microtubules and the growth of the heart. Here, we highlight a new role for microtubules in directing cardiomyocyte hypertrophy by altering protein translation and intercellular adhesion and discuss how these findings illuminate open questions in cardiac remodeling.

item.title: Nature Reviews Genetics: Decoupling cis and trans transcriptional influences
item.description: In this Journal Club article, Selin Jessa discusses a 2008 paper by Wilson et al. that used a transchromosomic mouse model to show that species-specific gene expression is determined by variation in cis sequence rather than in trans -acting factors.

item.title: Trends in Cell Biology: Mesenchymal stem cells: towering ambitions, shaky foundations
item.description: Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) have been a feature of stem cell research since the early 1990s. Despite long-standing questions concerning the identity, characteristics, physiological functions, and potential therapeutic uses of these cells, MSC studies are now published more frequently than those of any other stem cell type. Over the past decade, this increase in the MSC literature is attributable almost entirely to publications by scientists in China. Reviewing the history and present state of MSC research, we explore why this might be and propose steps that stakeholders in China and other countries might take to address what has become one of the more perplexing developments in contemporary stem cell research.

item.title: Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology: Molecular functions, cellular responses and pathological implications of the RNA modification N 6 -methyladenosine
item.description: This Review discusses how the RNA modification N 6 -methyladenosine (m 6 A) precisely regulates eukaryotic gene expression and orchestrates cellular stress responses, metabolic homeostasis and immunity. It also explores the pathological consequences of m 6 A dysregulation in brain disorders and cancer.

item.title: Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology: Why cells use many lipids when few will do
item.description: A synthetic minimal cell can survive with just two lipids, revealing that extensive lipid diversity is not essential for life. This Comment discusses our current understanding of why cells contain so many lipids and highlights future research avenues.

item.title: Trends in Genetics: An ancient genetic switch controls avocado flowering time
item.description: Heterodichogamy in avocado results in the coordination of female and male floral phases through reciprocal A and B flowering types. Recent evidence has identified SYNCHRONIZED DICHOGAMY MYB (SDMYB) as strongly associated with this polymorphism, revealing an ancient trans-specific system that has been maintained for over 42 million years and linking floral timing, reproductive polymorphism, and evolution.

item.title: Trends in Genetics: From Mendel’s peas to polygenic prediction
item.description: Polygenic risk scores (PRSs) aggregate genome-wide genetic variants into quantitative estimates of disease susceptibility. I describe how PRSs evolved from the early work of Mendel and Fisher and argue that they are ready for implementation in selected conditions within genomic learning health systems that iterate as evidence accumulates.

item.title: Trends in Genetics: Mitochondrial genome homeodynamics across scales
item.description: Mechanisms that maintain the mitochondrial genome, termed mitochondrial DNA homeodynamics, span vastly different spatial and temporal scales. A multiscale framework may help to reconcile seemingly disparate mechanisms, unifying canonical and emerging processes and providing a shared conceptual and mechanistic foundation for future investigations.

item.title: Trends in Cell Biology: Lipid droplet targeting at single-molecule resolution
item.description: Lipid droplet proteins can move from the endoplasmic reticulum to droplets through persistent membrane connections. A new single-molecule study reveals that accumulation is not only about access: protein sequence features tune residence on the droplet surface, revealing how confined mobility can lead to accumulation on the organelle (Mizrak et al.).

item.title: Nature Reviews Genetics: Small variant calling in the era of long-read sequencing
item.description: Long-read sequencing is expanding the scope of small-variant detection, enabling analysis of genomic regions that were previously difficult to interrogate. In this Review, the authors examine approaches for long-read small-variant calling across sequencing platforms and applications, highlighting advances in deep learning, assembly-based and pangenome-based methods, benchmarking strategies and future challenges.

item.title: Trends in Genetics: PEAK: a phenotype-based classification of genetic variants
item.description: Current variant classifications do not capture clinical severity relative to other pathogenic variants in the same gene. We propose phenotype-exceeding-(mono)allelic-knockout (PEAK) as a term for variants associated with a more severe clinical phenotype than that of heterozygous null alleles. This mechanism-independent designation may facilitate genotype–phenotype interpretation and identify candidates for allele-selective therapeutic development.

item.title: Nature Reviews Genetics: Towards equitable population epigenomics: implications for global health
item.description: Population epigenomic studies remain heavily skewed towards participants of European genetic ancestries, limiting the discovery and translation of DNA methylation associations across contexts. The Diverse Epigenetic Epidemiology Partnership outlines priorities for building a more equitable global epigenomics research agenda and improving the relevance of epigenetic insights for global health.

item.title: Nature Reviews Genetics: Towards a rational terminology for cell types
item.description: In this Comment, the authors outline how the lack of a consistent evolutionary framework for defining and naming cell types complicates comparisons across species and obscures questions of homology. As a solution, they propose that cell-type nomenclature be grounded in evolutionary theory by identifying conserved regulatory cores and explicitly incorporating phylogenetic origins into cell-type names.

item.title: Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology: Revealing the invisible transcriptome
item.description: The discovery of widespread expression of unstable promoter-associated transcripts has changed our understanding of genomic transcription activity.

item.title: Trends in Genetics: Design foresight and model humility for omics inference
item.description: Omics inference increasingly proceeds transcriptome-first: measure RNA, then ask how much biology can be extracted later. The ordering should be settled before the assay is chosen, not reconstructed from the data afterward. The first question is what the target requires to be directly observed; the second, what claims the data can honestly support. Design foresight means choosing assays, sampling, and orthogonal measurements based on the question and saying whether transcriptomics is primary, supporting, or insufficient for that claim. Model humility means refusing to promote computational output beyond what the data and assumptions can bear and writing measured, inferred, and predicted results in voices matched to their support. Using transcriptomics as the central case, we argue for question-first omics inference.

item.title: Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology: Ubiquitin phosphorylation opens a hatch to a code still largely undeciphered
item.description: The discovery of ubiquitin phosphorylation as a mitophagy activator pointed to ubiquitin being at the heart of a broad signalling code.

item.title: Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology: Scaling up measurements of the interactions that build condensates
item.description: Condensate partitioning by mRNA-display (CPmD) enables high-throughput assessment of protein (domain) propensity for condensate formation.

item.title: Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology: Atomic, structural and molecular insights into GPCR ligand binding and signalling
item.description: This Review explores the atomic, structural and molecular basis of G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR)-mediated signalling, highlighting recent insights into conformational changes associated with ligand recognition and interaction with downstream adaptors, and underscoring their importance for the development of therapeutics.

item.title: Nature Reviews Genetics: Gene regulation at the early human maternal–fetal interface
item.description: Human placentation establishes a dynamic maternal–fetal interface in which fetal trophoblast cells coordinate tissue remodelling, immune adaptation and resource exchange to support pregnancy. In this Review, the authors discuss how single-cell, spatial and functional omics are uncovering gene regulatory mechanisms underlying trophoblast differentiation and maternal interactions and how these insights are advancing understanding of healthy placentation and pregnancy disorders.

item.title: Nature Reviews Genetics: Histone acetylation finds its link to transcription
item.description: In this Journal Club, Liling Wan highlights a 1996 paper by Brownell et al. that linked a transcriptional coactivator to histone acetyltransferase activity, which contributed to the foundation of chromatin biology today, and reflects on the lessons it offers about the enduring value of curiosity-driven research.

item.title: Nature Reviews Genetics: Mapping genetic risk to regulatory networks at single-cell resolution
item.description: In this Tools of the Trade article, Yunlong Ma describes scMORE, a framework that integrates GWAS and single-cell multi-omic data to identify trait-associated regulatory networks in specific cell types and states.

item.title: Trends in Genetics: A complex relationship: pre-mRNA 3′ processing and transcription termination
item.description: Two molecular events occur at gene ends: 3′-end processing of pre-mRNA and transcription termination. Decades of studies have functionally coupled them, yet we discuss evidence that changes in these processes can occur in opposing directions. Acknowledging this paradox is necessary to gain a real understanding of how gene ends are shaped.

item.title: Nature Reviews Genetics: The African DSI DataBank: a federated infrastructure for Africa’s genomic and biodiversity data
item.description: The African DSI DataBank is a new federated platform designed to support African stewardship, governance and sharing of biodiversity and agricultural digital sequence information. This Comment outlines its architecture, rationale and roadmap for enabling African institutions to host, manage and contribute genomic and other biomolecular data types while retaining local control.

item.title: Nature Reviews Genetics: How cells remember sex
item.description: In this Journal Club article, Bruno Hudry discusses how Thomas Cline’s 1984 paper on the role of Sex-lethal in sex determination in Drosophila melanogaster illustrates the power of classical genetic experiments.

item.title: Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology: Engineering synthetic proteins to toggle function in response to kinase signals
item.description: In this Tools of the Trade article, Cao (Toettcher Lab) discusses the development of kinase-responsive phospho-switches that enable researchers to couple endogenous kinase signalling to activation of a synthetic protein actuator.

item.title: Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology: Towards a systematic understanding of the diverse subtypes, biogenesis and functions of large extracellular vesicles
item.description: Large extracellular vesicle (lEV) subtypes have diverse biogenesis, cargo, functions and roles in disease. This Review article provides an overview of lEV characteristics, highlights open questions in the field and indicates how a systematic approach towards lEV characterization assisted by emerging technologies will ensure reproducibility, advancing lEV research.

item.title: Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology: Chaperone-mediated autophagy in physiological homeostasis, disease and ageing
item.description: Chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA) is a selective lysosomal degradation pathway. Recent insights into its regulation, substrate repertoire and therapeutic modulation have revealed organ-specific functions and highlighted CMA as a therapeutic target in ageing and disease.

item.title: Nature Reviews Genetics: Is genome-wide epigenetic reprogramming a eutherian innovation?
item.description: New methylome data from marsupials indicate that genome-wide DNA methylation erasure is restricted to extraembryonic tissues. Ozren Bogdanovic discusses the implications of these findings for understanding the evolution and developmental functions of epigenetic reprogramming in mammals.

item.title: Nature Reviews Genetics: Decoding epithelial–mesenchymal transitions with multi-omics
item.description: Epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) is a dynamic cell-state transition that underpins embryonic development, tissue repair and ageing and is frequently co-opted in disease. In this Review, Narwade and Nieto discuss how single-cell, spatial and integrative multi-omics approaches, together with computational frameworks, are revealing EMT heterogeneity, trajectories, mechanisms and translational opportunities.

item.title: Nature Reviews Genetics: Inheritance and selection of the mitochondrial genome
item.description: Despite a high mutation rate and maternal inheritance, mitochondrial genomes remain remarkably stable across generations. This Review explores how the mitochondrial bottleneck and purifying selection shape mitochondrial DNA inheritance and examines the mechanisms that limit the transmission of deleterious variants.

item.title: Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology: Neutrality as the null hypothesis of biological evolution
item.description: A seminal paper that showed that genome complexity in multicellular eukaryotes is shaped more by genetic drift than by natural selection.

item.title: Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology: HoT self-blinking probes for chromatin imaging
item.description: In this Tools of the Trade article, Wang (Cosma Lab) and Zhang (Hongyan Sun Lab) describe the development of self-blinking HoT probes that are compatible with super-resolution microscopy and can be used to resolve nuclear architecture and chromatin.

item.title: Trends in Cell Biology: Handles on chromosome architecture
item.description: Cohesin organizes genome folding through loop extrusion, a process regulated by cofactors including NIPBL and PDS5. Recent studies by Wutz et al. and Shah et al. demonstrate that NIPBL promotes loop expansion in mammalian cells, whereas PDS5 restricts loop growth by facilitating NIPBL dissociation from cohesin. Together, these findings reveal a finely tuned mechanism governing genome folding.

item.title: Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology: Technological prominence alone does not justify leadership in SynCell governance
Trends in Genetics: How mutagenic are transposable elements?
item.description: Even though transposable elements (TEs) are known to be ubiquitous, studies on mutation rates often overlook this dynamic component of the genome. Fortunately, both our understanding of the mechanisms and assays of movement within and between lineages have expanded. In this review, we aggregate direct estimates of TE mutation rates from the literature to quantify the mutagenicity of mobile DNA. Overall, based on a subset of comparable studies, the mean rate of gain is 1.6 × 10−3 elements per copy per generation, an order of magnitude faster than the mean rate of loss (1.9 × 10−4). We discuss challenges for comparing rates across studies and outline the major genotypic and phenotypic consequences of TE movement. In conclusion, TEs can no longer be sidelined as ‘junk’ given the genetic variation they generate. Instead, we argue the role of TEs as an endogenous mutagen means they demand a more central place in mutation research.

item.title: Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology: p53 keeps a transcription–replication balance that prevents chromothripsis
item.description: p53 loss induces global increase of transcription that causes nucleotide shortage and replication stress, thereby driving formation of DNA double-strand breaks and chromothripsis.

item.title: Nature Reviews Genetics: Chromosomal chaos surrenders to logic
item.description: In this Journal Club, Kamila Naxerova reflects on two landmark studies by Knouse et al. and Davoli et al. that helped explain how disrupted epithelial tissue architecture promotes aneuploidy and why particular patterns of chromosome gain and loss recur across cancers.

item.title: Trends in Genetics: Preparing primary care professionals for genomics-informed healthcare
item.description: As genomics becomes increasingly mainstream, primary care will play a critical role in delivering genomics-informed healthcare. Drawing on our experience building a genomics education program for US physicians and nurse practitioners trained in primary care, we highlight that genomic capability requires education, workflow-integrated clinical support, and access to genetics expertise.

item.title: Nature Reviews Genetics: Machine learning and statistical methods for molecular quantitative trait loci
item.description: Molecular quantitative trait loci (molQTLs) provide key insights into how non-coding variants shape complex traits and disease. In this Review, the authors outline statistical and machine learning approaches for molQTL mapping and downstream analyses, including confounder correction, fine-mapping and colocalization, as well as the integration of pleiotropy, epistasis and causal mechanisms in molQTL models.

item.title: Trends in Genetics: DNA methylation: unifying framework for complex chronic conditions
item.description: Complex chronic conditions represent a growing health burden that is poorly understood and inadequately managed within current health systems. This review focuses on the potential of epigenetic DNA methylation to provide a pathway for better understanding of four closely related conditions: myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS), long COVID (LC), fibromyalgia (FM), and hypermobile Ehlers–Danlos syndrome (hEDS). These conditions have extensive overlapping symptoms, suggesting shared underlying pathophysiological mechanisms. Epigenetic regulation, particularly DNA methylation, provides a powerful framework for comparative and longitudinal studies across these clinically overlapping conditions. Here, we synthesise evidence from current DNA methylation studies in ME/CFS, LC, and FM, and consider how an integrated cross-condition approach could advance mechanistic insight, enable diagnostic stratification, and improve patient outcomes.

item.title: Trends in Genetics: Beyond gene editing: the age of chromosome-scale genome engineering
item.description: Genome engineering is moving from local sequence modification to manipulation of megabase-scale regions and whole chromosomes. This shift reflects the growing recognition that many biological functions and disease states are shaped by chromosome-scale features, including gene dosage across multiple loci, long-range regulation, chromatin context, replication timing, competition for limiting epigenetic factors, and three-dimensional genome organization. Here, we review the toolkit for chromosome-scale manipulation in higher eukaryotes, focusing on chromosome transfer, targeted chromosome elimination, and their integration into chromosome transplantation workflows. We discuss how these approaches, together with advances in large DNA assembly, synthetic biology, and genome-wide validation, are making chromosome-scale genome engineering an increasingly tractable experimental framework for understanding, building, and repairing genomes, while outlining the analytical requirements and current technical barriers that limit routine implementation.

item.title: Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology: Mechanisms and disease relevance of DNA break repair pathway choice
item.description: This Review focuses on the choice between homologous recombination and non-homologous end joining in DNA double-strand break repair. The antagonistic roles of 53BP1 and BRCA1–BARD1, the contribution of RNA–DNA hybrids and implications for targeting repair imbalance in cancer are discussed.

item.title: Nature Reviews Genetics: A Middle East collaborative for undiagnosed diseases
item.description: Undiagnosed disease networks advance the discovery of genes associated with rare diseases. However, a considerable gap in discovery remains, and genomic resources continue to exhibit population bias. A collaborative initiative in the Middle East could harness unique population structure, extensive family lineages and underrepresented genomic diversity to enhance local diagnostic capabilities and facilitate global gene discovery.

item.title: Nature Reviews Genetics: The many faces of malaria parasites
item.description: In this Journal Club, Elena Gómez-Díaz highlights two studies that established the Malaria Cell Atlas, demonstrating how single-cell transcriptomics can resolve parasite heterogeneity across development, transmission and natural infections to advance malaria research.

item.title: Nature Reviews Genetics: Gene regulatory mechanisms downstream of DNA methylation
item.description: In this Review, Buckley et al. discuss how DNA methylation is interpreted in mammals and plants, focusing on the reader proteins and transcription factors that bind to methylated DNA and the downstream mechanisms by which they regulate transcriptional and epigenetic states.

item.title: Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology: A practical guide to studying genome function using single-molecule genomics
item.description: Single-molecule genomics methods are used to study the activity of regulatory factors on individual DNA molecules genome-wide, thereby enabling quantification of molecular heterogeneity and co-occurrence of regulatory events. This Expert Recommendation article provides a practical guide for adopting single-molecule genomics and outlines best practices.

item.title: Trends in Genetics: African genomes are not a subset
item.description: Africa harbors more genetic variation than the rest of the world combined, but approximately 1% of genomes in major databases derive from individuals of African ancestry. This is not an equity problem; it is a scientific error that distorts drug dosing, degrades risk scores, and undermines precision medicine globally.

item.title: Trends in Genetics: Mitotic chromosomes: from the chromosome scaffold model to condensins and physical forces
item.description: Mitotic chromosome organization and assembly remain fundamental questions in genetics. Since the chromosome scaffold model proposed in 1977 highlighted the role of nonhistone proteins in determining chromosome shape and size, key nonhistone proteins, including condensins and topoisomerase IIα (topoIIα), have been shown to play critical roles in organizing chromosome axes and chromatin loops. Emerging evidence from biochemistry, imaging, and genomics suggests that mitotic chromosome assembly is a dynamic process driven by the interplay of condensin-mediated looping, topoIIα-dependent entanglement/disentanglement, and multiple physical forces, including electrostatic nucleosome interactions, linker histone H1, free Mg2+, and depletion attraction. In this review, we discuss how these mechanisms contribute to chromosome assembly and propose that interphase chromatin domains function as dynamic building blocks of mitotic chromosomes.

item.title: Trends in Cell Biology: Transcription elongation by RNA polymerase II: from regulatory complexity to disease
item.description: Transcription elongation by RNA polymerase II (Pol II) was originally considered as the monotonic addition of ribonucleoside triphosphates to the growing nascent RNA chain. However, multiple lines of evidence now indicate that transcription elongation is a regulatory hub in gene expression that requires an increasing number of elongation factors (EFs), dysregulation of which leads to pathologies. In this review, we provide a current view of the elongation phase of Pol II, focusing on mammalian cells. We describe the increasing complexity of the mechanisms that control transcription elongation. We examine the growing set of EFs, their functional roles, and their systemic implications in human disease. Finally, we discuss the emergence of EFs as promising therapeutic targets.

item.title: Trends in Cell Biology: The emerging cellular metal ions–immune axis in cancer
item.description: Cancer immunotherapy is frequently hindered by the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Although metal ions have been viewed as essential nutrients or cytotoxic payloads, emerging evidence reveals that they are potent immune modulators that orchestrate the cancer-immunity cycle. Here, we synthesize how ionic competition dictates immune cell plasticity and metabolic fate. We detail how metal ions regulate cell death pathways and immune signaling cascades, including the cyclic GMP-AMP synthase–stimulator of interferon genes and nuclear factor kappa B pathways, as well as immunological synapse formation and immune cell responses. Finally, we evaluate the clinical potential of targeting the metal ions–immune axis, from metallomic biomarkers, including Zrt-/Irt-related protein transporters and ion channels, to metallo-immunotherapy strategies. This framework provides a mechanistic roadmap for developing combination therapies to overcome immunotherapy resistance and harness the cellular metallome for precision oncology.

item.title: Trends in Genetics: Circular RNAs as central regulators of RNA stability
item.description: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are a class of covalently closed, single-stranded RNAs generated predominantly through back-splicing of pre-mRNAs. Unlike their linear counterparts, circRNAs lack free 5′ and 3′ termini, rendering them intrinsically resistant to exoribonucleolytic degradation and conferring exceptional stability. In addition, accumulating evidence has revealed that circRNAs actively participate in regulating the stability of other RNA species. This review explores the current understanding of intrinsic molecular features dictating circRNA stability. Furthermore, we emphasize recent progress on how circRNAs crosstalk with and regulate the stability of other RNA species, including mRNAs and microRNAs, through various mechanisms. Ultimately, we provide an integrated perspective for understanding circRNA-centered regulation of RNA stability.

item.title: Trends in Genetics: The study of evolvability in gene regulatory networks
item.description: Evolvability refers to the capacity of biological systems to generate heritable and adaptive phenotypic variation. Theoretical work has identified general principles linking gene regulatory network (GRN) architecture, including modularity and connectivity, to the generation of such variation, whereas empirical studies have uncovered its molecular basis in specific systems. Despite these advances, the two approaches have largely developed in parallel, with direct tests of theoretically derived hypotheses remaining rare. Recent advances in single-cell omics techniques, GRN inference, and experimental perturbation methods now provide opportunities for a closer link between theory and empirical research on evolvability. Here, we synthesise the main advances on this topic and outline potentially fruitful avenues for investigating how network structure and developmental dynamics shape evolvability across systems.

item.title: Trends in Cell Biology: ER-associated sorting links proteostasis to photosynthesis
item.description: Proteotoxic stress challenges multiple organelles, but how plants coordinate proteasome capacity with organellar function remains unclear. Langin et al. reveal that endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-associated sorting of NAC53/78 toggles these transcription factors between ER-associated degradation and nuclear activation, coupling proteasome induction to repression of photosynthesis-associated genes during stress.

item.title: Trends in Genetics: Trends in large-scale human population cohorts
item.description: As a foundational infrastructure of biomedical research, large-scale human population cohorts have undergone rapid progress over the past decades. Driven by advances in high-throughput omics technologies, widespread adoption of electronic health records, and the emergence of artificial intelligence, these cohorts now integrate deep molecular profiling with longitudinal real-world data at an unprecedented scale. This transformation has shifted cohort research from primarily descriptive association studies toward mechanistic discovery, refined risk stratification, and genetically informed therapeutic development. In parallel, cohort initiatives are expanding globally beyond Western populations, accompanied by increasingly diverse funding, governance, and data-sharing models. Here, we review the major transformative trends shaping large-scale human population cohorts and discuss how these resources are redefining disease biology, translational research, and the future of precision medicine.

item.title: Trends in Cell Biology: Vitamins tune cell death thresholds
item.description: Vitamins are essential micronutrients traditionally viewed as passive cofactors that sustain cellular homeostasis. Emerging evidence challenges this notion, identifying vitamins as active regulators of cell fate that tune the threshold for regulated cell death. Through coordinated control of redox balance, metabolic pathways, and signaling networks, vitamins shape cellular susceptibility to diverse death programs. Their effects are highly context-dependent, enabling both prosurvival and prodeath outcomes depending on dose, cell type, and metabolic state. Recent studies further uncover noncanonical mechanisms linking vitamins to lipid remodeling, membrane trafficking, and organelle integrity. Collectively, these advances establish vitamins as dynamic modulators of cellular vulnerability and highlight their potential as therapeutic targets for selectively manipulating cell death in disease.

item.title: Trends in Genetics: Rethinking evidence for epigenetic inheritance in human research
item.description: In multicellular organisms, epigenetic inheritance is a process by which traits induced by life experiences or environmental factors in a parent are passed to offspring without involving changes in the DNA sequence, but rather in the epigenome. While epigenetic inheritance is evident in many species, from plants to rodents, it remains unproven in humans because of biological barriers, methodological complexity, and the difficulty of disentangling environmental from social and genetic factors. The unique human context of prolonged parental care, as well as cross-generational cultural and societal effects, compounds these difficulties and highlights the need for clear criteria to assess epigenetic inheritance claims. This article aims to help the field move from cataloging biological markers to conducting rigorous human research by clarifying key concepts and defining testable criteria as a guiding framework.

item.title: Trends in Genetics: Everything, everywhere: FSHD as a model for complex genetic disease
item.description: Medical genetics can reveal how genetic variations shape human biology by addressing a critical question: how does a genetic lesion become a phenotype? Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD), exemplifies how a seemingly simple genetic lesion can affect multiple layers of cellular regulation, affecting ‘everything, everywhere all at once’.

item.title: Trends in Cell Biology: Microtubule function in pluripotent mouse embryonic stem cells
item.description: Cultured mouse embryonic stem cells can be maintained in a naïve pluripotent state, meaning the cells can give rise to all lineages of the embryo proper while self-renewing through rapid proliferation. This review summarizes recent advances in our understanding of the role of the microtubule (MT) cytoskeleton in pluripotency maintenance. We focus on intercellular bridge MTs, as these are prominent, long-lasting structures that arise during cytokinesis yet maintain the connection between dividing sister cells into the next cell cycle. We describe how MT stability sets cytokinesis duration and how this may influence pluripotency maintenance, division symmetry, midbody inheritance, and abscission. Together, these findings highlight an emerging paradigm: MTs are not merely structural scaffolds but active players in stem cell maintenance.

item.title: Trends in Genetics: Olduvai domains: humanity’s lucky brake
item.description: Neoteny—a developmental slowdown that results in the retention of juvenile traits into adulthood—has long been viewed as central to human brain expansion. Olduvai domains are proposed here to function as a dosage-dependent metabolic ‘brake’ that slows development via mitochondrial downregulation. Their human-specific hyperamplification, paired with NOTCH2NL accelerators and new metabolic insights, may solve a century-old evolutionary puzzle.

item.title: Trends in Genetics: Rethinking molecular evolution through protein language model embeddings
item.description: Protein language models compress protein sequences into high-dimensional embeddings that capture biochemical, structural, and functional constraints without explicit supervision. We highlight that these embeddings encode rich evolutionary information, enabling new geometry-based views of homology, divergence, and convergence, and calling for a synthesis between classical molecular evolution and systematic evolutionary embedding analysis.

item.title: Trends in Cell Biology: A 2026 perspective on neural stem cells and glial plasticity
item.description: Neural stem cells (NSCs) span a continuum of cellular states that share fundamental properties with their differentiated glial progeny. Recent single-cell studies have refined our understanding of the diversity within both NSC and glial populations, revealing a highly dynamic and interconnected landscape of cell identities. In this review, we examine the glial nature of NSCs, emphasizing their heterogeneity and the stem- and progenitor-like properties shared with the differentiated glia. We focus particularly on astrocytes and integrate evidence from invertebrate models demonstrating that glial cells possess an intrinsic capacity for neurogenesis. Together, these findings highlight areas of convergence between astrocyte plasticity and NSC-associated properties, with important implications for nervous system regeneration and brain cancer.

item.title: Trends in Cell Biology: KCTD10 resolves co-directional transcription–replication conflicts
item.description: Co-directional (CD) transcription–replication conflicts (TRCs) arise when the DNA replication and transcription machineries progress along the same DNA template. Although generally considered less severe than head-on (HO) TRCs, CD TRCs are now recognized as frequent and actively regulated events that influence genome stability. The Cullin 3–Potassium channel tetramerization domain containing 10 (KCTD10) ubiquitin ligase complex functions as a bivalent sensor that detects CD collisions and directs the nonproteolytic ubiquitination of the elongation factor TCEA2, transiently remodeling RNA polymerase II to permit replisome bypass. This sensing-driven remodeling reframes CD TRCs as dynamic decision nodes where replication and transcription priorities are continuously negotiated, highlighting how conflict geometry, ubiquitin signaling, and genome maintenance are functionally integrated.

item.title: Trends in Cell Biology: Endoplasmic reticulum architecture in liver metabolic regulation
item.description: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is a central hub for essential cellular processes, including lipid and glucose metabolism, protein folding, calcium homeostasis, and detoxification. The ER exhibits a complex architecture, comprising multiple subdomains such as the nuclear envelope and the peripheral ER, which is further organized into sheets, tubules, three-way junctions, and contact sites. Both ER form and function are highly adaptive, with a robust capacity to respond to changes in environmental cues such as nutritional states. Here, we discuss remodeling of ER shape - as a fundamental mechanism of metabolic regulation, which enables the diversification and fine-tuning of metabolic function in physiology, while also representing a potential point of vulnerability during metabolic stress. We focus on the liver, a central organ in systemic energy homeostasis, and examine how hepatic ER morphology and its dynamic interorganelle interactions are reorganized in response to nutritional fluctuations and how this remodeling reflects on metabolic function.
